subject: Trying to subset data in RMR2 for individual analysis, analogy to RHIPE

messages.author: 9febcbf26d2ccc5b
messages.subject: Trying to subset data in RMR2 for individual analysis, analogy to RHIPE
parts:
Hello,

The group behind RHIPE has a statistical approach for big data called “Divide and Recombine”.  In nutshell, you divide your data into subsets.  In a map step,  each subset becomes a value with a unique key.  In the next map step, the estimation procedure is applied to each value.  In the reduce step, the means of the estimates are taken.

I have written an algorithm for RHIPE that tests to what degree the speed of the procedure depends on the size of the subset.  The total data is a matrix with N observations and P + 1 columns, that is then split up into subsets that each have M rows, for a total of R = N/M subsets (M chosen so that R is an integer).  Assume N is a very large number.

Each of these subset then becomes a value so you have R keyvalue pairs.   So while the total amount of data N remains the same, the number of key value pairs varies, and the size of each value varies. 

In the RHIPE algorithm, the data is predicted and subsetted in the first map, then glm.fit() is applied to each subset/value (P predictors and 1 response).

I am trying to write the same algorithm for RMR2, and do so in a way that the speed for RHIPE and RMR2 can be compared fairly.

The problem is creating subsets in RHIPE is easy because within a for loop, you can simulate a single subset and make it a value in a single key-value pair.  For example (R-like pseudocode, not actual RHIPE code);
map (
    for (i in 1:r) {# r is number of subsets
        mat <- (generate a matrix with m rows and p+1 columns)
        key <- i
        value <- mat
        collect(key, value) # keyvalue pairs are created iteratively
    }
)



Then in the fitting step we have;
map(
    for (i in seq_along(map.values){
        mat <- map.values[[i ]]    #iterates through all the values from last map
        coef <- glm.fit(mat)$coefficients
        key <- 1  # the same key for each subset
        value <- coef
        collect(key, value)
    }
}



Finally, these are summed up in reduce (in practice you would use mean, but sum is easier to code because its associative)
reduce(
    r <- sum(number of coefficients estimates)
    sum.coef <- sum(coefficients estimates)
    key <- 1
    value <- c(r, sum.coef)
    collect(key, value)
)



Since RMR2 doesn’t support looping, and simulating all the data at once could create problems with some data structures, I plan to read in data from the HDFS. 

My question is, how should I represent subsets in RMR2?  I first tried was to simulate the data, as one big data.frame, create a factor that represents subset membership, and use the by() function to apply glm or glm.fit to the data using subset as a grouping variable.  That didn’t work because of the memory constraints of a data.frame.  I think this will work if I read in the data from the HDFS, but I am not sure if treating each row as a value as RMR2 likes to do equivalent treating subsets as values.   I also thought of creating a big list with matrix subsets as values and wrapping that with the keyval() function, then using glm.fit in lapply().  But from what I read RMR2 either doesn't support or is resistant to doing that.

Can you offer some suggestions?

On Sun, Apr 7, 2013 at 2:05 AM, Robert Ness <rober...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello,

The group behind RHIPE has a statistical approach for big data called “Divide and Recombine”.
I read about it.  It's not clear to me what it is other than renaming and reselling map reduce to a statistical audience.

In nutshell, you divide your data into subsets.  In a map step,  each subset becomes a value with a unique key.  In the next map step, the estimation procedure is applied to each value.  In the reduce step, the means of the estimates are taken.

Great, how would that work for the max or for quantiles? If you want to read some research on the subject, I recommend  the paper "mergeable summaries" . Taking average of subset estimates, even babies can do that, but what are the statistical properties? You know, old fashioned bias and variance questions? If I take the average of maxes, we are just averaging the bias of each estimate. For the same computational cost, we can take the max and reduce that bias. Let's not trivialize parallel programming.

I have written an algorithm for RHIPE that tests to what degree the speed of the procedure depends on the size of the subset.  The total data is a matrix with N observations and P + 1 columns, that is then split up into subsets that each have M rows, for a total of R = N/M subsets (M chosen so that R is an integer).  Assume N is a very large number.

Each of these subset then becomes a value so you have R keyvalue pairs.   So while the total amount of data N remains the same, the number of key value pairs varies, and the size of each value varies. 

In the RHIPE algorithm, the data is predicted and subsetted in the first map, then glm.fit() is applied to each subset/value (P predictors and 1 response).

I am trying to write the same algorithm for RMR2, and do so in a way that the speed for RHIPE and RMR2 can be compared fairly.

If it's down to a speed comparison, I think you are missing the point.  rmr2 is  within 20% of java speedwise on some realistic test cases and we are working to extend that across other use cases. It's worth working on that because the resulting programs are small and elegant, no need for pseudo code to hide the boilerplate. If RHIPE has achieved Java parity speedwise, hats off but it doesn't really move the needle. There are other issues like compatibility with different distros, IO formats, it's  not just, A is faster than B, use A, drop B. Then Java or C++, if not assembly, win every time. And you wouldn't even bother building abstractions into libraries, because there is a penalty to pay, you'd rather program at the lowest level possible all the time.

The problem is creating subsets in RHIPE is easy because within a for loop, you can simulate a single subset and make it a value in a single key-value pair.  For example (R-like pseudocode, not actual RHIPE code);
map (
    for (i in 1:r) {# r is number of subsets
        mat <- (generate a matrix with m rows and p+1 columns)
        key <- i
        value <- mat
        collect(key, value) # keyvalue pairs are created iteratively
    }
)

map = 
  function(a,b)
         function (k) keyval(1:r, lapply(1:r, function(i) generate.mat(i))

Then in the fitting step we have;
map(
    for (i in seq_along(map.values){
        mat <- map.values[[i ]]    #iterates through all the values from last map
        coef <- glm.fit(mat)$coefficients
        key <- 1  # the same key for each subset
        value <- coef
        collect(key, value)
    }
}

map = 
  function(k,v)
     keyval(1, lapply(v, function(mat) glm.fit(mat$coefficients))
 
I frankly don't see where the problem is. Of course without a test case, I may be missing something.

Finally, these are summed up in reduce (in practice you would use mean, but sum is easier to code because its associative)
reduce(
    r <- sum(number of coefficients estimates)
    sum.coef <- sum(coefficients estimates)
    key <- 1
    value <- c(r, sum.coef)
    collect(key, value)
)

reduce = function(k,vv) keyval(1,parallel.sum(vv))

I am not sure what your sum of coefficients does but if it is an element by element sum you can implement it as Reduce('+', vv) or as an rbind followed by a colSum, the latter should be faster.
Since RMR2 doesn’t support looping,

How did this fantastic statement originate? Please don't confuse my users with these statements. rmr2 allows looping because it's just R. It uses side effects less than Rhipe because it aims to be closer to an R (functional) style than a Java style of programming.

and simulating all the data at once could create problems with some data structures, I plan to read in data from the HDFS. 

My question is, how should I represent subsets in RMR2?  I first tried was to simulate the data, as one big data.frame, create a factor that represents subset membership, and use the by() function to apply glm or glm.fit to the data using subset as a grouping variable.  That didn’t work because of the memory constraints of a data.frame.  I think this will work if I read in the data from the HDFS, but I am not sure if treating each row as a value as RMR2 likes to do equivalent treating subsets as values.   I also thought of creating a big list with matrix subsets as values and wrapping that with the keyval() function, then using glm.fit in lapply().  But from what I read RMR2 either doesn't support or is resistant to doing that.

Can you offer some suggestions?

See the above code. The problem is that you are trying to translate Rhipe into rmr2. As somebody who's spoken a non-native language for a third of my life, translating is not the right approach, you have to think in the new language. I suspect the same applies here. The rmr2 way is "very functional" so to speak and vectorized through and through. It is more memory intensive, no doubt, but I don't understand your consideration well enough to offer very precise advice. Which ones of the following is applicable

1) create one matrix per map call, or a small number,
2) apply glm right away, do not send your whole data set through the shuffle phase, more so when it's generated


X = from.dfs(mapreduce(
  to.dfs(1:number.of.matrices),
 map = function(k,v) keyval(v%%number.of.keys, list(coeff(glm(generate.matrix())(
reduce = function(k,vv) keyval(k, parallel.sum(vv))))


If you are reading the data, instead of generating it then it is

mapreduce(input,
map = function(k,v) keyval(sample(1:number.of.groups, nrow(v))
reduce  = function(k,vv) glm(vv))

Then you do further processing in memory. I am sure I am missing something, but you may be able to start with this and make it do what you need.


Antonio
